When you use puzzle as a verb, it means to cause someone to feel confused because they cannot understand something — or, from the other direction, to think hard and carefully about something you find difficult to understand.

The key idea is this: it's not just any confusion. It's the kind where your mind keeps turning something around, asking "Why? How? What does this mean?" — and the answer refuses to come easily.
The Two Directions It Works In

1. Something puzzles someone

Here, a thing or situation is the cause of the confusion. The thing acts on the person.

  • Her silence puzzled him. (He couldn't figure out why she wasn't talking.)
  • The missing key puzzled the whole family. (No one could explain where it went.)
  • His odd behaviour puzzled the doctors. (They couldn't make sense of it.)

Notice: the thing doing the "puzzling" is not a person trying to confuse someone on purpose. It's simply that the thing is hard to explain. The confusion arises naturally.

You'll also see this in the passive form — "someone is puzzled by something" — which means the same thing but puts the focus on the person:

  • She was puzzled by his sudden change of mind.
  • I was puzzled by the strange note on my desk.

2. Someone puzzles over something

Here, a person is actively working hard to understand something difficult. The focus is on your own mental effort.

  • He puzzled over the strange message for hours.
  • She sat quietly, puzzling over what the dream could mean.
  • The child puzzled over the riddle, trying every possible answer.

When you "puzzle over" something, you are sitting with a problem, turning it around in your mind, examining it from different angles — but the answer still doesn't come easily. It suggests slow, concentrated, careful thinking.

To puzzle something out means to eventually find the answer or meaning of something through hard, patient thinking. It implies you started confused — but kept going until you worked it out.

  • It took me a while, but I finally puzzled out what he was trying to say.
  • She puzzled out the solution on her own, without any help.
  • He stared at the map for a long time before puzzling out the right route.

The phrase "puzzle out" has a satisfying quality to it — it suggests effort followed by a moment of understanding. You wrestled with something difficult, and you won.

This is important for truly understanding the word: being puzzled is not the same as being scared or upset by something you don't understand. It is closer to curious, engaged confusion. Your mind is alert and working, but the answer eludes you.

Compare it to how you feel when you're solving a puzzle (the noun) — you're interested, you're thinking, but you haven't found the answer yet. The verb carries that same sense of active, curious, slightly frustrated mental engagement.

There are several words that are close in meaning, and knowing the differences will sharpen your understanding:

  • Confuse — a general word for making someone unable to understand. Broader and more neutral. The instructions confused me. Doesn't imply as much mental effort or curiosity.
  • Perplex — very close to puzzle. Slightly more formal, and sometimes carries a hint of distress or anxiety along with the confusion. The diagnosis perplexed the specialist.
  • Baffle — stronger than puzzle. When something baffles you, you are completely stumped — you have absolutely no idea how to explain it. How he escaped completely baffled the investigators.
  • Mystify — implies that something seems almost magical or impossible to explain. Her ability to predict events mystified everyone around her.
  • Bewilder — suggests a feeling of being lost or disoriented, not just confused about one thing. Often implies the confusion is overwhelming. The crowded, noisy city bewildered him.

Puzzle sits somewhere in the middle — more active and engaged than "confuse," but not as extreme or overwhelming as "baffle" or "bewilder."

Here is a quick summary of everything:

  • Something puzzles you → a thing causes you confusion because you can't explain or understand it.
  • You are puzzled by something → same meaning, passive voice.
  • You puzzle over something → you think hard and carefully about something you can't understand.
  • You puzzle something out → after hard thinking, you finally reach an understanding or solution.

The emotional quality is curious and engaged, not frightened or overwhelmed. The mental quality is active and effortful — puzzlement is not passive; your mind is always working on the problem.

One sentence to remember it by:

When something puzzles you, your mind keeps circling a question it can't answer — and when you puzzle it out, you've finally found your way through.
